item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in Hawaii has ruled in favor of environmental groups opposing a seabed mining lease sale in American Samoa, finding that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act when it approved the sale.

The lease sale was set for Thursday, California time. The judge did not specifically issue an injunction canceling the sale, although the agency consultation was voided.

Faʻasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaiʻi, represented by the environmental law organization Earthjustice, filed a lawsuit after the National Marine Fisheries Service determined that the Marine Minerals Administration lease sale was not likely to adversely affect endangered species.

The court ruled that the Fisheries Service accepted the administration’s definition of the “agency action” as the lease sale itself, not post-lease activity.

“By doing so, [National Marine Fisheries Service] only considered the preliminary effects of the lease sale and did not even attempt to consider potential effects of post-leasing activities. NMFS’s cramped, expedited, informal consultation is apparently unprecedented in the context of leasing on the [Outer Continental Shelf],” the ruling stated.

In a news release Wednesday, Earthjustice said the ruling was a win for the people of American Samoa, “as well as the whales, sharks, and sea turtles who call the waters surrounding these islands home.”

“It recognizes that the law requires the government to understand the full repercussions of its actions before letting this untested industry destroy one of the most pristine parts of the ocean on the planet,” said Chris Eaton, Earthjustice attorney.

Last year, the Trump administration vowed to fast-track seabed mining to give the United States access to critical minerals deep in the ocean.

A lease sale for up to 69 million acres east and west of the Mariana Islands is set for Dec. 16. The American Samoa and Mariana Islands leases involve areas within the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone.

On Tuesday morning, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration held a virtual public hearing on an application from a company that wants to look for polymetallic nodules in international waters.

Eco Minerals, previously known as Deep Sea Rare Minerals, wants to explore an area of seabed about 700 miles east-northeast of Guam, as well as eight areas in the Eastern Pacific’s Clarion-Clipperton Zone.

Those who testified in the hearing urged regulators to deny the license, arguing that the deep-sea ecosystem is not well understood and mining could cause long-term harm.

item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service is urging residents of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands to remain weather-aware as drought conditions develop across the region and El Niño keeps the potential for late-season tropical activity above normal.

A dry season-like pattern is expected to persist across the Marianas through the weekend, bringing mostly sunny skies, spotty showers and strengthening trade winds, according to the National Weather Service in Guam. Fire danger on Guam has risen to the high category as rainfall remains limited and vegetation continues to dry out.

Despite the dry conditions, Marcus Landon Aydlett, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Guam office, said residents should not overlook the threat of tropical cyclones.

"The risk for late-season tropical cyclones remains elevated through the end of the year and into early 2027 compared with other years," Aydlett said, citing the ongoing El Niño pattern.

No tropical cyclone development is expected during the next seven days, but forecasters said El Niño conditions could continue to influence weather across the western Pacific through the remainder of the year.

The weather service said a wetter pattern may develop later next week and continue into December, providing some relief to drought-affected areas across Micronesia. Residents with low or empty water catchments are encouraged to collect rainwater when showers occur.

item.content:encoded:
The Marianas Audubon Society is calling volunteers to sign up for its annual Christmas Bird Count. The project is split into two days to cover the northern and southern parts of Guam.

At 6:15 a.m. on Dec. 19, the society will meet at the Yona carabao statue next to Buenas Market to conduct its southern bird count. In the afternoon, the society is hoping to gain access to Naval Base Guam, where volunteers must bring their passport and Real ID in order to participate and access the base.

At 7 a.m. on Jan. 2, 2027, the society will meet at Shirley’s Diner in Tamuning to conduct its northern bird count. In the afternoon, members hope to access Andersen Air Force Base, where volunteers will need to provide documentation weeks prior to the event date. If you wish to access the base for the northern count, volunteers must email marianasaudubon1983@gmail.com before or by Nov. 30.

The bird count is meant to assist in identifying and counting the bird population on Guam. This program was established on Guam in 1983 and is in partnership with the National Audubon Society, which provides insight into the health and status of bird populations throughout the United States.

Registration is open from now until Nov. 30. To sign up, email marianasaudubon1983@gmail.com

item.title: Mary Peltola flips Alaska's Senate seat into Democrats' column
item.description: Stay connected: The NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has won Alaska's U.S. Senate contest, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.
item.content:encoded:
Stay connected: The NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola has won Alaska's U.S. Senate contest, toppling the Republican incumbent, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Peltola bested Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in one of the country's most closely watched Senate campaigns. With her victory, Democrats will have 56 Senators in the upcoming Congress.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting for its general election, but Peltola won a majority of Alaskans' first-place votes, meaning no ranked-choice calculation was needed.

Peltola's victory flips a Senate seat in a state that President Trump carried in each of the last three presidential elections. Trump won Alaska by 13 percentage points in 2024.

The race was roiled in its final days by new allegations, reported by The New York Times , that Peltola's team was involved in efforts to recruit another candidate to the race, Dan J. Sullivan, to try to siphon votes from the incumbent.

Peltola's campaign denied involvement in the second Sullivan's candidacy. NPR has not independently confirmed the reporting.

A federal judge rejected a lawsuit by the Trump administration to block certification of the results if the incumbent Sullivan lost.

Peltola is from Bethel, a western Alaska hub city of about 7,000 that's not connected to the state's limited road system. She is the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Alaska since 2008 and will be the first Alaska Native to serve in the U.S. Senate.

Peltola campaigned mostly on the themes that Democrats around the United States focused on: affordability, healthcare costs and accusing Republicans of flagrant corruption. The cost-of-living argument has special salience in rural Alaska, where groceries and gas can be double or triple the cost elsewhere.

With a campaign motto of "fish, family, freedom," she also spoke of the salmon crisis on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers , an issue that propelled her to statewide prominence in her first U.S. House race in 2022. In this campaign, she pitched herself as the candidate who would crack down on industrial-scale pollock fishing in the Bering Sea. Alaskans increasingly blame that industry for catching and wasting salmon, halibut and other species.

Sullivan is a Marine Corps veteran elected to the Senate in 2014 who previously served as Alaska's attorney general. He is a strong advocate for augmenting the military and Coast Guard's presence in Alaska.

Sullivan has also been a steadfast ally of Trump. The president flew to Wasilla last month and held a rally to boost Sullivan's candidacy. But Trump's approval ratings in Alaska and nationally have plunged since 2024, driven largely by opposition to the Iran war and angst over high prices.

The election results suggest that unpopularity was a drag on Republican incumbents.

The U.S. Justice Department plans to appeal the dismissal of its lawsuit, which sought to block the certification of Alaska's Senate race if Sullivan lost.

The department asked the judge to stop state officials from certifying election results to allow for an investigation into whether voters were confused by having two candidates named Dan Sullivan appear on Alaska's ranked-choice ballot.

The judge in that case concluded that such a court order would "clearly violate" Alaskan voters' right to a secret ballot. Alaska's governor has also ordered an investigation into the race.

Ballot stacking and promoting spoilers are generally legal in Alaska and have been relatively common.

Super PACs aligned with Republicans and Democrats spent more than $2 million on "ballot composition" efforts in Alaska this year, sometimes to elevate people who don't live in Alaska, including a federal inmate in New York.

But the Trump administration, the incumbent Sullivan and other Republicans claim that the goal of Dan J. Sullivan's candidacy was to trick voters.

The Justice Department said in a statement that "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."

Preliminary race results suggest other candidates did not act as spoilers. Peltola, as of Sunday, had more votes than the other three candidates combined.

item.title: Families push more air safety measures as FAA grapples with system improvements

item.content:encoded:
We turn now to Capitol Hill, where aviation safety was the headline today. Family and friends of those who died in that horrific midair collision over Washington, D.C., last year gathered outside the Capitol to push for more safety measures. Meanwhile, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy continued to push Congress for billions of dollars to modernize the air traffic control system following Friday's nationwide ground stop. NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose has been following all of this and joins me now in the studio. Joel, I talk to you so much lately.

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Hi, Scott. Good to see you again.

DETROW: Let's start with the families of the crash victims. You were at this event outside the Capitol. What was it like?

ROSE: This was organized by the family and friends of the 67 people who died last year when an Army Black Hawk helicopter crashed into a passenger jet over the Potomac River just as the plane was about to land at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. Today they stood on the West Lawn of the Capitol building in the shape of the outline of the plane with empty chairs signifying their lost loved ones. Audrey Patel talked about losing her husband, Vick (ph) Patel, who was on American Airlines Flight 5342, while she was pregnant with their first child.

AUDREY PATEL: I missed him at the first ultrasound when I heard our baby's heartbeat for the first time. I missed him during the birth of our son. I miss him for all the firsts that he was so excited about, the big moments, and I miss him in all the small moments.

ROSE: Besides the family members, we also heard from the secretary of transportation, senators from both sides of the aisle, safety investigators, aviation union leaders, all pushing for changes to aviation safety laws so that other families don't have to go through what these families did.

DETROW: I mean, it sounds like there is broad support for these changes. Where does the effort stand?

ROSE: Yeah, the midair collision prompted a lot of safety recommendations from the National Transportation Safety Board. One thing in particular that the NTSB called for is wider use of a safety system called ADS-B In and Out. Investigators say if those systems were fully in use, that that could have prevented the crash. The Senate unanimously approved a version of the bill that would require wider use of those systems, but it stalled out in the House, where it came up just a few votes short after the Pentagon pulled its support at the last minute.

Families of the victims want to see a compromise bill that could pass the House and the Senate in the lame duck session. Senator Ted Cruz said today there is agreement in principle with lawmakers in the House, but Cruz also said that there are still some details to be worked out with the House Armed Services Committee. So not clear exactly whether this deal will get done during the lame duck session, but family members said today they are encouraged by that progress.

DETROW: And this event today, this reminder of this terrible accident nearly two years ago, happened just days after this massive story and equipment meltdown that led to that rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. What's the latest there?

ROSE: Yeah. After the event outside in the West Lawn, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy went up to the Capitol, where he met with Senate Republicans to push for more money to modernize the nation's air traffic control system. Duffy is asking Congress for $50 billion, though, after the lunch, he sounded - after that meeting, he sounded willing to maybe settle for a bit less.

SEAN DUFFY: I'll take what I can get. And I will work with the Congress to make sure that we do the highest priorities first. And I would hope that they don't do that to me, but I'll take what I can get, and I'm going to build with whatever they give me.

ROSE: Congress has already given more than $12 billion - allocated more than $12 billion to modernize the air traffic control system. Democrats say they want more accounting of how the administration is spending that money before they approve more. And even Republicans sound pretty skeptical about this $50 billion number.

DETROW: Have aviation regulators taken any action since this meltdown?

ROSE: Yeah, the Federal Aviation Administration is still investigating exactly what caused the meltdown. The FAA says workers were upgrading old copper wires to fiber optic cables when a router made by the company Juniper Networks began flooding the network with information. The FAA administrator said today they have suspended the use of this particular router and disabled the ones that are already installed while the investigation continues. It's still not clear if this was a faulty router, an installation error, something else, but the FAA says they're trying to get to the bottom of it.

DETROW: NPR transportation correspondent Joel Rose. Thank you.

(SOUNDBITE OF KENDRICK LAMAR SONG, "SING ABOUT ME, I'M DYING OF THIRST") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.content:encoded:
Say that last Thursday, you were trying to email your boss about a business trip this week. But Microsoft Outlook was down, so you had to wait to send that email till Friday. But on Friday, a fiber-optic cable replacement crashed the routers that deal with air traffic, and that held up nearly all departing flights nationwide. When that finally sorted out, and you rebooked a flight on Monday, United Airlines had a brief system outage that further delayed your takeoff, at which point you went to your banking app to see how much all this was costing you, but that was briefly down yesterday too.

UNIDENTIFIED REPORTER: AI, United, Chase bank.

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: It's life. It's life. When you're big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It's fine.

PFEIFFER: President Trump downplayed all the outages today. Although, speaking of being big and powerful, NPR has confirmed that the classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its own internal communications has been having issues today. We have so many questions about all of this, which is why we have called Dmitri Alperovitch. He's cofounder of the cybersecurity technology company CrowdStrike, and he's founder of the Alperovitch Institute for Cybersecurity Studies at Johns Hopkins University. Thank you for coming on the program.

DMITRI ALPEROVITCH: Thanks for having me.

PFEIFFER: At this point, is there any evidence that all these incidents are connected in any way or maybe are tied to cybercrime?

ALPEROVITCH: No. And I understand that people are very suspicious. Obviously, all of these events happening almost every day is very strange. But these things happen. And, you know, one of Murphy's laws, of course, is that never attribute anything to malice that which is adequately explained by incompetence. I think a lot of these things happening because people are actually in the midst of a lot of upgrading right now.

There is, of course, the AI threat. A lot of vulnerabilities are being found by these AI models. And as a result, a lot of companies, a lot of organizations across the world, are trying to patch these vulnerabilities as quickly as possible. So we're going through this patch apocalypse right now. And sometimes when you're updating systems, we all know things can go wrong, and I think that's partly what's happening here.

PFEIFFER: So are we having this collision of our extreme reliance on technology, overtaxed, often aging systems that, as you said, periodically need updating. We know that cyberattacks are common. We know that rogue AI is a fear. Are we seeing the fragility of the system all coming together?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, these are all different systems. So there's no question that we're much more reliant on technology. So when things go down now, it causes much more inconvenience for us. You know, in the old days, it was easier to get into, perhaps, your bank and - physically and withdraw money, and now we're relying much more on online banking and those sorts of things. So the impact to us is much greater, but these things have always happened. But I do think there's something to the idea that, right now, it's happening more because everyone is trying to update their systems before they can get hacked by these AI models.

PFEIFFER: I was going to say updates are a fact of life, but you're saying particular updates happening now because of the risks of AI that are becoming apparent - people trying to get ahead of that.

ALPEROVITCH: That's right. More vulnerabilities have been discovered this year than the last 30 years combined. So that's as a result of AI looking at these software packages, identifying new vulnerabilities. So enterprises, government agencies are, right now, completely flooded with reports that you need to update your systems because there's another critical vulnerability that has just been discovered.

PFEIFFER: Could that mean that we're going through a rough patch right now, but it will be temporary, or is this going to be an ongoing symptom of our modern age?

ALPEROVITCH: I think the next 12 to 18 months are going to be very rough, not just because of the update cycles, but also because some people will not upgrade in time, and, of course, there will be more hacks as a result. But I think we'll come out on the other end in a much safer way because a lot of the software - your Microsoft Office, your, you know, infrastructure software - will all get much more secure.

PFEIFFER: It's a bit of a cat and mouse game in terms of technology and upgrades and bad actors looking for vulnerabilities. So does that suggest that this is just going to be the ongoing game of cat and mouse that lasts forever?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, this has been the life in cybersecurity for the last 40 years, and I don't think that's going away. As long as there are people out there with malicious intentions, whether it's nation states or criminals or hacktivists, we're going to have problems. And, of course, the biggest vulnerability remains the user, not your computer system, because people fall for social engineering attacks, for phishing scams, and that I expect will continue to be the case.

PFEIFFER: And people have weak passwords, and they might not use two-factor authentication. What - to give some practical advice for people, are we all just helpless victims of this, or what basic things should people be doing to try to protect themselves?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, in terms of your own systems, yes, update it automatically. Make sure that you're fully patched whenever a vulnerability comes out. Make sure, as you said, you have two-factor authentication and strong passwords. But when it comes to this infrastructure going down, you know, we're all observers here and unfortunately sometimes victims because if your bank goes down, there's not a lot you can do.

PFEIFFER: When you looked at the FAA national ground stop on Friday, which we now know appears to have been related to a upgrade happening in Arkansas where something didn't go well and, suddenly, the whole system goes down, is there, in general, not a way to prevent small mistakes happening in isolated areas from crashing an entire system?

ALPEROVITCH: Well, usually, there is, and this was a surprise that there's sort of this one weakness in the system that could take the whole thing down. Usually, there's redundancies. Now, the problem is that a lot of these systems have gotten so complex, with so many layers to them over the years, that it's very, very difficult to understand where those points of failure might be. And hopefully, this is one area where AI might actually help us to identify these problems ahead of time.

PFEIFFER: Oh, that's interesting. Many people are so focused on the negatives of AI and the fear that it will go rogue and cause chaos. But you're saying here's a reminder that it could help us in this situation.

ALPEROVITCH: Absolutely. I think it's going to do some amazing things for us in lots of different areas, but there's no question, like, every technology, it comes with downsides.

PFEIFFER: It sounds to me like your industry has work for infinity, basically.

ALPEROVITCH: There's a lot of job security in cybersecurity.

PFEIFFER: (Laughter) In terms of an overall parting thought, is there any way that we as individuals can be trying to minimize the impact of this on our lives, whether it's reducing our dependency on tech, increasing our protections? What's your advice for those who want to throw their hands up in the air?

ALPEROVITCH: Everyone should focus on resiliency in their daily life. Always have some cash lying around just in case you can't get your money withdrawn from an ATM for a period of time. You know, stockpile some water, stockpile some groceries. I think those are prudent things to do in any scenario. Of course, there could be other catastrophes, weather-related, terrorism, etc. that you want to be prepared for. So that's always a good thing to do.

PFEIFFER: That is Dmitri Alperovitch, a cybersecurity expert and CEO of the Silverado Policy Accelerator. Thank you.

ALPEROVITCH: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

item.title: Take a look, it's in his book: LeVar Burton writes a memoir
item.description: As kid, LeVar Burton never daydreamed about being on TV. He wanted to be a priest. Growing up in Sacramento, Calif., Burton attended a Catholic school and admired how his favorite priest was "a source of calm for people in their lives." "That's what service looked like to me at the time. It was nothing more than wanting to be useful ... in a way that made sense to me," Burton says.
item.content:encoded:
As kid, LeVar Burton never daydreamed about being on TV. He wanted to be a priest. Growing up in Sacramento, Calif., Burton attended a Catholic school and admired how his favorite priest was "a source of calm for people in their lives."

"That's what service looked like to me at the time. It was nothing more than wanting to be useful ... in a way that made sense to me," Burton says.

The priest fantasy is one of many revelations Burton makes in his new memoir, Take My Word for It. As it turns out, while Burton was attending college at the University of Southern California, he auditioned for — and landed — the role of Kunta Kinte, the central character in the landmark 1977 miniseries Roots.

Based on Alex Haley's historical novel , the series grappled with the legacy of slavery — and launched Burton in a different direction. His character, a West African warrior who is enslaved and taken to America, touched him deeply.

"I felt, and still feel, very aligned to Kunta," Burton says. "I knew everything I needed to know about that character, about that kid, and I had no problem expressing it, because there's a part of me that had been waiting for a long time to speak out on the state of race in America."

In 1983, Burton began hosting Reading Rainbow , a PBS kids' show that he also executive produced. The show, which ran until 2006, was designed to combat the "summer slide" kids experience when not in school, and to encourage enthusiasm for reading. Burton says it's not uncommon for adults to approach him in tears to tell him what the show meant to them.

"There are a couple of generations of adults now who grew up on Reading Rainbow who consider it a part of their personal ethos," Burton says. "It has become one of the biggest surprises of my life that I … have had the impact that I've had."

Burton also touched audiences with his portrayal of Geordi La Forge on Star Trek: The Next Generation, and later Star Trek: Picard. In his new memoir, Take My Word For It , he writes about life both inside and outside of his iconic roles, and the unexpected turns he's experienced along the way.

On his friendship with his Star Trek co-star Patrick Stewart

We laughed a lot — one of the main ways we communicated with each other was laughter. I was asked to give a quote after Patrick passed and I say, in part, of all of the dames and knights I've ever known, he was, at his core, the silliest. ...

When we were together, he allowed the silly part of himself to be present. And that was a huge compliment and a huge factor in our success because at the very beginning, he took us to the woodshed one afternoon and said, "Listen, we are not here to laugh, we're not here to play, we're here to work." And we all just laughed at him, knowing that if we were going to survive this series, if we're gonna survive this experience, that laughing and having fun needed to be an essential part of it.

On his Star Trek character Geordi La Forge, who is initially blind but eventually receives ocular implants

People tell me all the time that they love Geordi and that they were always glad when Geordi got human eyes and I'd say, "Why? Human sight is a downgrade for Geordi. He sees the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Why would he wanna just limit himself to the narrow band of human vision?" … I loved Geordi for a lot of reasons, pretty much the most of which is his ability to see the world in different ways.

On the advice he received from Fred Rogers when he was doing Reading Rainbow

I really wanted to know what his secret sauce was and, as it turns out, it was nothing more than being your authentic self. ... I think that Fred Rogers was a bona fide saint, really. Because I haven't encountered that many human beings, very few human beings, who live so firmly in their purpose and part of that purpose is joyful. At the same time, Fred was a very joyful man, a very joyful human being. And I know through my experience with him that he felt fulfilled and wouldn't want to be doing anything other than what he was doing, and I learned from that.

During the process of shooting Reading Rainbow , at that point in my life, I was reading the trades, and had my eye on what was going on over there, and who was getting this job, and who was giving that job and, "Why aren't I getting those jobs?" rather than just being fine with where I was. I didn't understand at the time how important what we were doing on Reading Rainbow was, what its future impact would be on generations of human beings. As it turns out, I was in the right place at the right time. I was exactly where I needed to be, and Fred was, in part, an anchor for me in that regard.

On learning from veteran actors on the set of Roots

My very first day as a professional actor, Cicely Tyson played my mother, Dr. Maya Angelou played my grandmother. Day one. Day one! And the thing is that I wasn't intimidated at all. Perhaps I should have been, but I wasn't. I knew I belonged there. And because I knew I belonged there, they assumed I belonged there, too. And that opened up a space between them and me, the elders I'm talking about, that paid major, major dividends, not just during the filming of Roots but throughout the whole of my career.

Everything that I employ on a daily basis as a professional actor — the foundations of it — I learned from being in the makeup trailer with Louis Gossett Jr. and Hari Rhodes and Dr. Maya. It was a real education, and not just the mechanics, but the behavioral aspects, how we treat one another, how we treat every member of the crew with respect — [the] humanity, the human aspect of doing what it is we do, and how we go about it.

On going by "Bob" all through childhood to assimilate in his white schools

If nothing else, it gave me a level of comfort that I had a handle, an entry point to people that I liked. I enjoyed being Bob. It worked for me, it fit. ... In [my mother] Erma Gene's house, you spoke the King's English… Family and friends, those were the places where it was safe to reveal those other aspects of us, but in public, there was a demeanor — it was incumbent upon me to act through being respectable to white society. And not just respectable, but ... a kind of excellence that not many of them were able to produce.

It was our job to assimilate and to assimilate at the highest levels that we possibly could in as a way of proving our worthiness to the rest of American society. That was the game at the time, that was the game. And I'm lucky enough to have lived through that era into the next incarnation of us, where we could show our excellence without the other trappings. We could just be excellent, right? We didn't have to be excellent with a caveat, right. We could be excellent. And whether or not they accepted that or not, right, that's not the point. The point is my expression of who I am and making my family proud.

On discussing his bipolar diagnosis in the book

I didn't want to leave this part out. It's easy to imagine that LeVar Burton just leads this charmed life. And in many respects, that's true. But that's not the whole story. And everybody has brain chemistry that we need to deal with. I'm not special in that regard. I struggle. I want to continue to live and be here and be productive. I need to take my brain chemistry into consideration and part of the book was recognizing that we inherit our brain chemistry just like we do our physical DNA from our parents and just like we do our spiritual DNA from our ancestors. These things are, in part, bestowed upon us, and it's really incumbent upon us and important to turn around and take it on, to acknowledge it and to deal with it.

Anna Bauman and Thea Chaloner produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.
